title: Referendums
objective: After this level you can explain direct votes on a single question.
summary: A referendum puts one question to voters; an initiative starts with a citizens' petition. New Zealand chose MMP by referendum in 1993. Bulmer weighs benefits and risks; questions must be clear.

cards.headline: In 1988, Chile's ruler called a vote to keep himself in power. He lost.
cards.body: Augusto Pinochet, Chile's authoritarian ruler, held a referendum to extend his term. He unexpectedly lost, and his regime collapsed shortly after. One yes-or-no question turned out to be very powerful. So who gets to ask it?

cards.headline: One question, straight to the voters
cards.body: A referendum gives people a direct vote on a specific issue, sent to them by a parliament, president or government. A citizens' initiative works the other way round: the people start it, usually with a petition signed by a set number of people. Results can be binding or only advisory, though advisory votes are usually treated as binding in practice, especially if decisive.

cards.headline: Voters choose the rules
cards.body: Remember Level 63's New Zealand? It settled its voting-system argument by asking the voters. In a binding referendum in 1993, 53.9% chose MMP over first-past-the-post. The people chose the method that would count their own votes.

cards.headline: Worth it? The debate
cards.body: Elliot Bulmer's primer for International IDEA weighs both sides. For: you vote on one measure on its merits, not a party's whole package. Against: voters may react to unrelated things, like how popular the leaders are; frequent votes cause fatigue; rulers can use referendums to fake legitimacy. The Venice Commission adds a rule: the question must be clear, not misleading, and must not suggest an answer.

cards.headline: Referendums: decided
learned: Referendum: a direct vote on a question put by government
New Zealand chose MMP by referendum in 1993
Benefits and risks; questions must be clear and fair

questions.prompt: What makes a citizens' initiative different from a referendum?

options.label: It is always advisory
options.rationale: Both can be binding or advisory.

options.label: Only parliament may vote in it
It is started by the people, usually through a petition
It asks several unrelated questions at once

questions.explanation: A referendum is sent to voters by governing institutions; an initiative is started by the people, typically by petition.

questions.prompt: Which is a criticism of referendums listed in Bulmer's IDEA primer?

options.label: Voters may react to unrelated things, like leaders' popularity
They let people vote on one measure on its merits
They always favour whoever wrote the question
options.rationale: That isn't one of his listed criticisms.

options.label: They are illegal under the Venice Commission
options.rationale: The Commission sets standards, not bans.

questions.explanation: Bulmer notes voters may be swayed by unrelated factors, frequent votes cause fatigue, and rulers can fake legitimacy.

questions.prompt: Level 16 said direct democracy now lives inside representative systems as specific tools. How does a referendum fit that?

options.label: Voters elect representatives to decide for them
A court settles the question on the voters' behalf
options.rationale: A referendum sends the issue to voters, not judges.

options.label: All laws must pass an open-air assembly first
options.rationale: That's a Landsgemeinde, not a single referendum.

options.label: Voters decide one specific issue themselves

questions.explanation: A referendum is a direct vote on a specific issue: one of direct democracy's tools, used inside a representative system.
